Neonates of Gammarus roeselii emerge from the maternal brood pouch at a body length of roughly 0.152 cm [Lb = roughly 0.152 cm], a diminutive size that nonetheless allows the newly released individuals to begin grazing on epiphytic biofilms immediately. The corresponding wet weight at birth is recorded as 0.123 milligrams [Wwb = 0.123 milligrams], reflecting the modest yolk reserves available to the developing embryo. These initial measurements are critical for understanding the early growth trajectory of this amphipod in lowland riverine habitats, where food availability can fluctuate markedly with seasonal algal blooms. The total length at birth is notably consistent across populations in Central Europe, suggesting strong canalization of the embryonic developmental program.

In contrast to the neonatal size, the ultimate total length attained by adult females of this species reaches 1.204 cm [Li = 1.204 cm], a dimension that positions G. roeselii as a medium‑sized gammarid within the Danube catchment. This asymptotic female length is accompanied by an ultimate wet weight of 59.1 milligrams [Wwi = 59.1 milligrams], which represents the maximal body mass recorded among gravid individuals in the population. The relationship between length and weight in these mature females follows a typical allometric pattern, and the attainment of this ultimate size generally requires multiple moulting events occurring over many months.

Sexual maturation in female Gammarus roeselii is characterized by a distinct pubertal moult, at which point individuals first develop functional oostegites. The total length at puberty has been estimated at 0.68 cm [Lp = 0.68 cm], representing roughly fifty‑six percent of the ultimate female length. The corresponding wet weight at puberty is 10 milligrams [Wwp = 10 milligrams], a threshold below which reproductive activity is not observed. These pubertal values indicate that females invest substantially in somatic growth before initiating gamete production, a pattern typical of amphipods from unpredictable environments.

The developmental timing of Gammarus roeselii is strongly temperature‑dependent. At a constant water temperature of 10.2 °C [T = 10.2 °C], the maximum lifespan computed for individuals from the river Fischa population is approximately 570 days [am = approximately 570 days], a duration that encompasses a single winter diapause and two active growing seasons. When the water temperature is elevated to 12 °C [T = 12 °C], the time since birth at puberty is accelerated to 204 days [tp = 204 days], indicating that even modest thermal differences can substantially compress the pre‑reproductive period and potentially alter the demographic structure of local populations.

Reproductive output in this amphipod species is also tightly linked to thermal regime. At a controlled temperature of 20.6 °C [T = 20.6 °C], the age at birth, or the time required for embryonic development within the brood pouch, is just 11.5 days [ab = 11.5 days], which is rapid for a gammarid of this body size. Under identical thermal conditions, females produce approximately 62.7 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 62.7 eggs per clutch] and can produce a brood every 11.5 days [F_R_i = brood every 11.5 days], yielding a high potential for population increase during warm summer months, a trait that has likely facilitated its successful invasion of many Central European watercourses.
